quote: In all these cases, every point of view is correct. It all depends upon what you consider to be moving.
apply: For probability/price charts, clearly label and allow toggling between fixed benchmark and moving market/portfolio-relative baselines.

principle: Visible signifiers for interactive controls
quote: We expect to find some visible signal, a signifier, for the correct operation: a plate, an extension, a hollow, an indentation— something that allows the hand to touch, grasp, turn, or fit into.
apply: On dark dashboards, give every clickable chart element, filter, and order control a persistent visible affordance—outline, icon, or label—so users do not have to hunt for interactivity.

principle: Constraints must be perceivable, not just present
quote: Although they do have physical constraints to prevent improper insertion, it is often extremely difficult to perceive their correct orientation
apply: Make binary market controls visually explicit, such as a high-contrast Yes/No segmented toggle with labels, instead of relying on subtle shape or orientation cues.

principle: Solve the root need rather than patching the old form
quote: A superior solution would be to solve the fundamental need—solving the root need.
apply: Prioritize implied probability, payout, liquidity, and time-to-resolution above raw order-book clutter; move secondary metrics into expandable drilldown panels.

principle: Respect cultural color conventions
quote: Red is the culturally defined standard for a brake light, which is placed in the rear.
apply: Reserve red for negative/loss and green for positive/gain in charts and P&L, use neutral blue/gray for informational states, and validate colorblind-safe palettes.

principle: Use natural mappings between controls and data
quote: If two switches control two lights, the left switch should work the left light; the right switch, the right light.
apply: Align controls with their effects: place the time-range selector directly above the chart, outcome filters next to the outcome list, and the order ticket adjacent to the selected market.

principle: Follow codified conventions and standards for trust
quote: Sometimes these conventions are codified into international standards, sometimes into laws, and sometimes both.
apply: Use familiar financial and prediction-market conventions for chart types, order-book sides, timestamps, and labels to reduce learning cost and build trust.

principle: Use visible signifiers and affordances so users can see what to do and where.
quote: The best push bars offer both visible affordances that act as physical constraints on the action, and also a visible signifier, thereby unobtrusively specifying what to do and where to do it.
apply: Make Buy, Sell, and Resolve actions explicit at the relevant market row or order panel with labels/icons and placement, not color alone.

principle: Base dashboard structure on observed user tasks.
quote: A usable design starts with careful observations of how the tasks being supported are actually performed
apply: Organize the dashboard around prediction-market tasks like scanning odds, comparing contracts, and managing exposure rather than around available data widgets.

principle: Use natural mapping between controls and what they affect.
quote: Match the layout of the lights with the layout of the switches: the principle of natural mapping.
apply: Keep contract/outcome order identical across watchlist, chart legend, order ticket, and position table so users can map rows to trades without relearning.

principle: Do not force multi-dimensional data into one-dimensional lists.
quote: there is no way they can map naturally to the two-dimensional, horizontal placement of the lights in the ceiling.
apply: Use 2D charts like scatterplots, heatmaps, or matrices for relationships among markets, probabilities, and time rather than only stacked lists.

principle: Do not let aesthetics undermine usability.
quote: The focus on aesthetics may blind the designer (and the purchaser) to the lack of usability.
apply: In dark mode, verify contrast, font size, and tabular numerals for dense tables/charts before adding neon accents or decorative glow.

principle: Respect known conventions to build comfort and trust.
quote: Known cultural norms can create comfort and harmony. Unknown norms can lead to discomfort and confusion.
apply: Use familiar finance conventions for color semantics, number formatting, and spacing consistently across charts and tables to reduce misinterpretation.

principle: Organize controls by user activity, not by data source or device
quote: In many cases it is better to have switches that control activities: activity-centered control.
apply: Group dashboard filters and order actions by trader workflows (e.g., 'research', 'trade', 'risk') rather than separate panes for order book, news, and positions.

principle: Consolidate related controls to avoid cognitive interruption
quote: It is a horrible cognitive interruption to the flow of the talk to go back and forth among the screens
apply: Place price chart, order book, and trade ticket in one view so users don't switch tabs to place or adjust a prediction-market order.

principle: Allow manual overrides without cancelling the active task
quote: invoking the manual settings should not cause the current activity to be canceled.
apply: When a trader manually adjusts chart scale or theme, keep the selected market and open order ticket intact.

principle: Use forcing functions to prevent high-risk errors
quote: Forcing functions are a form of physical constraint: situations in which the actions are constrained so that failure at one stage prevents the next step from happening.
apply: Require confirmation or a two-step sequence before submitting a large trade or moving funds on a prediction market.

principle: Use lockouts to disable dangerous actions
quote: a lockout prevents someone from entering a space that is dangerous, or prevents an event from occurring.
apply: Disable or clearly lock the trade button when a market is halted, resolved, or the wallet has insufficient collateral.

principle: Respect established financial conventions to build trust
quote: The interpretation of a perceived affordance is a cultural convention.
apply: Use familiar market conventions (green/red P&L, candlesticks, bid/ask) and avoid novel chart interactions without signifiers.

principle: Follow established conventions unless a change is vastly superior.
quote: Consistency in design is virtuous. It means that lessons learned with one system transfer readily to others. On the whole, consistency is to be followed.
apply: Use familiar market-dashboard conventions—green/red/neutral semantics, standard time-axis direction, and consistent order-book interactions—across every prediction-market panel.

principle: Avoid mixed systems and inconsistent interaction models.
quote: Mixed systems are confusing to everyone.
apply: Do not mix probability formats such as 0–100 and 0–1, or click versus hover interactions, across cards, charts, and order tickets.

principle: Make affordances visibly suggest their action.
quote: If you want the faucet to be pushed, make it look as if it should be pushed.
apply: Design Yes/No outcome selectors and trade controls as obvious tappable segmented controls or buttons, not ambiguous text links.

principle: Provide rapid, direct feedback for every action.
quote: Feedback in the use of most faucets is rapid and direct, so turning them the wrong way is easy to discover and correct.
apply: Instantly animate probability/price updates, hover states, and order previews so users can see the effect of filters and trades immediately.

principle: Minimize delay between controls and the data they affect.
quote: the delay between turning the faucets and the change in temperature can be quite long
apply: Place filters and controls adjacent to the chart or table they modify, and show a streaming/latency status if prediction-market data updates lag.

principle: Expose the variables users actually care about.
quote: We control exactly the variables of interest, and the mixing spout solves the evaluation problem.
apply: Surface probability, volume, liquidity, and time-to-resolution directly in the dashboard, with integrated controls, instead of forcing users to derive them.

principle: Map visual encodings to users' mental models, not backend mechanics.
quote: The standards should reflect the psychological conceptual models, not the physical mechanics.
apply: In dark prediction-market dashboards, encode higher probability as up/green and lower as down/red across price charts, order books, and outcome tiles, even if the API stores odds inversely, and label axes to match users' expectations.

principle: Make control dimensions and directional meanings explicit to avoid ambiguous mapping.
quote: The difficulty lies in a lack of standardization of the dimensions of control, and then, which direction of movement means what?
apply: For filters, sliders, and chart controls, always label both the dimension (liquidity, volume, time) and direction (↑ increase, ↓ decrease) so users never have to guess what a drag or toggle changes.

principle: Preserve visible affordances, signifiers, discoverability, and immediate feedback.
quote: Visible affordances and signifiers
apply: Use high-contrast interactive cues (hover/focus rings, legends, tooltips) on dark data-dense charts and tables, and show instant feedback for every action (loading, applied filters, last updated) to make functionality discoverable.

principle: Standardize interaction and visual conventions when other solutions fail.
quote: If all else fails, standardize.
apply: Adopt consistent conventions for Yes/No colors, buy/sell sides, chart zoom/pan, and filter placement across all prediction markets; this reduces cognitive load and lets users transfer knowledge between markets.

principle: Balance standardization with flexibility to avoid hindering future development.
quote: Standards simplify life for everyone. At the same time, they tend to hinder future development.
apply: Build a fixed design system for core prediction-market data (prices, probabilities, volumes), but allow configurable layouts/themes so new market types and data sources can be added without breaking familiar patterns.

principle: Use sound or explicit non-visual feedback to prevent silent failures and maintain trust.
quote: The absence of sound can mean an absence of knowledge, and if feedback from an action is expected to come from sound, silence can lead to problems.
apply: For critical dashboard events (order fill, resolution, stale feed, disconnection), provide optional distinct audio/desktop alerts and always show persistent visual status; never let sync failures or stale data be silent.

principle: Alerts should both notify and orient users about what changed, where, direction, and magnitude.
quote: Orientation. The sound will make it possible to determine where the vehicle is located, a rough idea of its speed, and whether it is moving toward or away from the listener.
apply: Toast and alert components should include market name, outcome side, price direction, delta magnitude, and timestamp instead of a vague 'Market moved' message.

principle: Frequent updates must be calm and non-annoying; reserve aggressive warnings for rare critical events.
quote: Because these sounds will be heard frequently even in light traffic and continually in heavy traffic, they must not be annoying.
apply: Use subdued inline color badges, sparklines, and row highlights for continuous price changes; reserve modals, flashing, and saturated red for liquidation or resolution-critical events.

principle: Standardize core visual semantics but allow limited individualization for brand or tracking.
quote: Standardization is necessary to ensure that all electric vehicle sounds can readily be interpreted. If they vary too much, novel sounds might confuse the listener.
apply: Keep colors, chart axes, price-direction conventions, and iconography consistent across all markets; vary only brand accents or market logos, never semantic colors.

principle: Design systems to prevent and contain human error, not punish users.
quote: When people err, change the system so that type of error will be reduced or eliminated. When complete elimination is not possible, redesign to reduce the impact.
apply: Add trade previews, confirmation for high-stakes orders, undo for filters/layout changes, and clear validation to prevent costly misclicks.

principle: Surface underlying causes, not just proximate events, in data views.
quote: Root cause analysis is intended to determine the underlying cause of an incident, not the proximate cause.
apply: Let users drill from a price spike into order-book depth, recent news, volume, liquidity, and resolution criteria rather than showing only the changed number.

principle: Support resumption after interruptions because interruption causes error.
quote: Interruptions are a common reason for error, not helped by designs and procedures that assume full, dedicated attention yet that do not make it easy to resume operations after an interruption.
apply: Persist filters, scroll position, selected market, and workspace state, and provide a 'resume last view' affordance and recent activity trail.

principle: Design must prevent errors, not blame users
quote: If the system lets you make the error, it is badly designed. And if the system induces you to make the error, then it is really badly designed.
apply: In order tickets, enforce constraints and clear previews so a mistap cannot submit an invalid or catastrophic trade; show slippage/fees before confirmation.

principle: Reduce precision demands
quote: But people aren’t very good at great precision. We frequently make errors when asked to type or write sequences of numbers or letters.
apply: Replace free-text numeric entry for price/size with steppers, sliders, and tick-sized presets; auto-format probabilities and contracts.

principle: Design for time stress
quote: A major cause of error is time stress.
apply: Keep live prices, spreads, positions, and P&L in a sticky top strip; surface urgent alerts and one-click cancel/close without burying controls.

principle: Separate execution slips from planning mistakes
quote: Slips occur when the goal is correct, but the required actions are not done properly: the execution is flawed. Mistakes occur when the goal or plan is wrong.
apply: Use undo/confirm/disable-mistap safeguards for order execution, and separate scenario/provenance panels for market thesis and probability assumptions.

principle: Avoid action-similarity slips
quote: Some slips result from the similarities of actions. Or an event in the world may automatically trigger an action.
apply: Make YES/NO, buy/sell, and cancel/submit controls visually and spatially distinct; avoid identical button shapes/colors and adjacent keyboard shortcuts.

principle: Account for expert automaticity
quote: An interesting property of slips is that, paradoxically, they tend to occur more frequently to skilled people than to novices.
apply: For power-user shortcuts and dense dashboards, add persistent mode/status indicators plus undo or final confirmation for destructive market actions.

principle: Differentiate controls and displays by purpose
quote: Designers need to ensure that controls and displays for different purposes are significantly different from one another.
apply: Use distinct shapes, colors, and label styles for Yes/No, Buy/Sell, and order types; never reuse identical pill buttons for opposing actions.

principle: Avoid identical opening steps in divergent workflows
quote: Designers need to avoid procedures that have identical opening steps but then diverge.
apply: Make trade flows for different market actions branch visually from the first click, with distinct ticket headers and color accents.

principle: Reduce simultaneous objects to prevent selection errors
quote: Similarly, the more objects present at the same time, the more likely the error.
apply: Use progressive disclosure and tight grouping in dense dashboards; show only relevant controls per panel and hide secondary actions.

principle: Minimize steps and add vivid reminders
quote: One is to minimize the number of steps; another, to provide vivid reminders of steps that need to be completed.
apply: Keep order entry short, show persistent step/status breadcrumbs, and auto-save drafts before confirmation.

principle: Make modes visible or avoid them
quote: Mode error is really design error. Mode errors are especially likely where the equipment does not make the mode visible
apply: Display a persistent mode chip/banner for chart interval, order type, live vs. simulation, and use distinct borders/backgrounds for active modes.

principle: Support conceptual models for interpretation
quote: Here, conceptual models are essential in guiding development of the plan and interpretation of the situation.
apply: Use consistent chart encodings, axis labels, legends, and resolution-criteria tooltips so traders can interpret probability, liquidity, and outcomes without guesswork.

principle: Display system state coherently and graphically
quote: Provide as much guidance as possible to ensure that the current state of things is displayed in a coherent and easily interpreted format—ideally graphical.
apply: Use charts, sparklines, and color-coded status tiles as the primary dashboard layer, not raw tables.

principle: Show alternative explanations and interpretations
quote: in a way that is easy to assimilate and interpret, as well as to provide alternative explanations and interpretations.
apply: Pair every market prediction with bull/bear evidence, source links, and explicit uncertainty rather than a single confidence number.

principle: Keep goals, plans, and evaluation continuously visible
quote: ensure that all the relevant information is continuously available. The goals, plans, and current evaluation of the system are of particular importance and should be continually available.
apply: Use a persistent sticky panel for watchlist, open positions, thesis, and last-reviewed timestamp so interruptions do not erase context.

principle: Support pattern matching with past analogues
quote: People usually decide by taking the current situation and matching it with something that happened earlier.
apply: Surface comparable historical markets, event timelines, and outcome distributions beside the live price chart.

principle: Manage contradictory information overload
quote: In complex situations, the problem is too much information: information that both supports the decision and also contradicts it.
apply: Use progressive disclosure, filters, and aggregated views, and visually flag conflicting signals instead of hiding them.

principle: Guard against single-diagnosis lock-in
quote: Once the mistaken diagnosis is made, all information from then on is interpreted from the wrong point of view.
apply: Add neutral framing, alternate-hypothesis toggles, and one-click reset/reframe controls to reduce anchoring on one narrative.

principle: Error-proof critical inputs rather than relying on user vigilance.
quote: Poka-yoke translates as “error proofing” or “avoiding error.”
apply: Constrain order entry with valid tick sizes, side/price presets, and disabled controls for impossible combinations so users cannot submit malformed trades.

principle: Use checklists to reduce slips and memory lapses in complex, high-stakes tasks.
quote: Checklists are powerful tools, proven to increase the accuracy of behavior and to reduce error, particularly slips and memory lapses.
apply: Add a compact pre-trade checklist that verifies market, side, size, price, liquidity, and resolution rules before final submission.

principle: Design high-risk confirmation as a paired read-execute workflow.
quote: It is always better to have two people do checklists together as a team: one to read the instruction, the other to execute it.
apply: For large orders or market resolutions, require a maker-checker confirmation with distinct roles and visible sign-off.

principle: Avoid forced sequential workflows unless the task truly requires them.
quote: In general, it is bad design to impose a sequential structure to task execution unless the task itself requires it.
apply: Let users fill dashboard filters, watchlists, and order fields in any order, and persist skipped steps instead of forcing a linear wizard.

principle: Track skipped or incomplete items persistently in electronic workflows.
quote: This is one of the major benefits of electronic checklists: they can keep track of skipped items and can ensure that the list will not be marked as complete until all items have been done.
apply: Show unresolved required fields or review steps as persistent chips, and keep final submit disabled until they are resolved.

principle: Surface errors and anomalies early so problems can be caught before harm.
quote: If errors can be caught, then many of the problems they might lead to can often be avoided.
apply: Use inline validation, stale-data warnings, thin-liquidity badges, and anomaly flags with plain-language explanations before confirmation.

principle: Use clear signifiers and constraints to make market direction and state self-evident.
quote: with the green dot indicating the direction in which the key needed to be turned: I added signifiers to the doors.
apply: Color-code Yes/No and Buy/Sell actions with paired text/icons and directional arrows in order tickets, depth ladders, and position rows so users can read market direction at a glance.

principle: Prevent dangerous actions with forcing functions and poka-yoke constraints.
quote: Covering emergency or critical switches with a cover to prevent accidental triggering is another poka-yoke technique: this is obviously a forcing function.
apply: Require two-step confirmation or hard limits for large orders, withdrawals, and irreversible settlement actions; lock critical controls behind an explicit review state.

principle: Add common-sense sensibility checks before executing high-impact trades.
quote: Do sensibility checks. Does the action pass the “common sense” test?
apply: Warn or block when order size or price deviates sharply from current market levels, enforce max notional limits, and show expected payout/risk before submit.

principle: Design for quick error detection through continuous, visible feedback.
quote: Errors do not necessarily lead to harm if they are discovered quickly.
apply: Show real-time order/fill status, position changes, and P&L impact in persistent dashboard regions, with an audit trail so mistakes are caught before they compound.

principle: Make actions reversible, or make irreversible actions harder to perform.
quote: Make it possible to reverse actions—to “undo” them—or make it harder to do what cannot be reversed.
apply: Provide undo/cancel for pending orders and drafts; for final settlement or withdrawal, use confirmation steps and cooling-off delays.

principle: Build trust through neutral, transparent provenance and oversight-free reporting.
quote: NASA is a neutral body, charged with enhancing aviation safety, but has no oversight authority, which helped gain the trust of pilots.
apply: Surface verifiable data provenance in the dashboard: source, timestamp, resolution oracle, and audit trail for every market and metric, avoiding unexplained numbers.

principle: Preserve and reveal resumable state after interruptions
quote: To resume, it is necessary to remember precisely the previous state of the activity: what the goal was, where one was in the action cycle, and the relevant state of the system.
apply: Persist the selected market, open order draft, chart interval, and watchlist position when users return; show a subtle “resume where you left off” strip.

principle: Reduce forced multitasking and simultaneous monitoring
quote: all the evidence points to severe degradation of performance, increased errors, and a general lack of both quality and efficiency.
apply: Consolidate market alerts and price movements into a prioritized queue instead of making users scan many live tiles at once.

principle: Prevent alarm overload and competing warnings
quote: Most can be ignored anyway because they tell the operator about something that is already known. Each competes with the others to be heard, interfering with efforts to address the problem.
apply: Tier alerts by severity, suppress already-known or duplicate market events, and keep only one high-priority alert region visible.

principle: Use progressive disclosure and constraints to block errors
quote: Another is to use separate modules, so that any control not directly relevant to the current operation is not visible on the screen, but requires extra effort to get to.
apply: Hide advanced order types, leverage, and settlement controls behind a deliberate panel so they cannot be triggered during routine trading.

principle: Make destructive or high-impact actions reversible
quote: Perhaps the most powerful tool to minimize the impact of errors is the Undo command in modern electronic systems, reversing the operations performed by the previous command, wherever possible.
apply: Provide undo or a short cancel window for order cancellation, position close, and watchlist deletion rather than irreversible one-click actions.

principle: Confirm by showing both action and object clearly
quote: A better check would be a prominent display of both the action to be taken and the object, perhaps with the choice of “cancel” or “do it.”
apply: In trade confirmations, display market name, side, size, price, probability, and maximum loss together—not just “Confirm order.”

principle: Run sensibility checks on anomalous order sizes.
quote: Intelligent systems would take note of the normal size of my transactions, querying if the amount was considerably larger than normal.
apply: For large prediction-market orders, compare the stake/size to the user's typical activity and require an explicit confirm step showing potential loss, payout, and liquidity impact before execution.

principle: Provide perceptible feedback for the action and the resulting state.
quote: provide perceptible feedback about the nature of the action being performed, then very perceptible feedback describing the new resulting state
apply: After placing or cancelling an order, immediately update the order ticket, positions, balance, and order book with a high-contrast success/error state so dark-mode users can see the result without scanning.

principle: Make errors reversible.
quote: coupled with a mechanism that allows the error to be undone.
apply: Include a prominent undo/cancel affordance for trades, watchlist edits, and filters—such as an undo toast or cancel window—so slips do not become permanent positions.

principle: Eliminate modes or make them highly visible and distinct.
quote: Mode errors can be eliminated by the simple expedient of eliminating most modes and, if this is not possible, by making the modes very visible and distinct from one another.
apply: Avoid ambiguous order-type/leverage modes; if modes persist, use a persistent high-contrast badge and distinct color/label near the order button to show the active mode.

principle: Differentiate similar controls to prevent description-similarity slips.
quote: Rows of identical controls or meters is a sure recipe for description-similarity errors.
apply: In dense dashboard tables and chart toolbars, differentiate buttons, tabs, and toggles with unique icons, labels, and spacing rather than uniform icon-only controls.

principle: Use layered safeguards and multi-signal risk alerts.
quote: Design redundancy and layers of defense: that’s Swiss cheese.
apply: For high-stakes actions, combine independent safeguards—anomaly checks, confirmation summaries, 2FA, audit logs—and surface a prominent banner when multiple risk signals (thin liquidity, high volatility, large position) coincide.

principle: Bridge the Gulf of Execution and Evaluation
quote: Bridge the two gulfs, the Gulf of Execution and the Gulf of Evaluation. Make things visible, both for execution and evaluation.
apply: In a dark dashboard, show an order/trade preview with expected payout, fees, and probability before submit, then immediately confirm filled/cancelled state with persistent visual feedback.

principle: Keep operational knowledge in the world
quote: Put the knowledge required to operate the technology in the world. Don’t require that all the knowledge must be in the head.
apply: Pin contract resolution rules, oracle source, expiry, and price-to-probability notation in the UI so users need not memorize them; use hover/tooltips for dense cells.

principle: Use constraints and natural mappings
quote: Use the power of natural and artificial constraints: physical, logical, semantic, and cultural. Exploit the power of forcing functions and natural mappings.
apply: Map market prices to an intuitive 0–100¢ probability scale with a consistent color ramp and constrain order inputs to valid ranges; disable or warn on impossible trades.

principle: Design for inevitable error and reversibility
quote: Assume that every possible mishap will happen, so protect against them. Make actions reversible; make errors less costly.
apply: Make orders cancelable/undoable, require high-friction confirmation for large or irreversible actions, and show max loss/risk before execution.

principle: Make critical system and mode status unmistakable
quote: the design of the navigation system didn’t make this apparent.
apply: Never hide live/delayed/simulated/stale data status behind tiny labels; use high-contrast persistent status chips or banners in the dark header.

principle: Build resilience through foresight and risk anticipation
quote: One measure of resilience is therefore the ability to create foresight—to anticipate the changing shape of risk, before failure and harm occurs
apply: Surface scenario charts, liquidity/depth warnings, oracle/resolution risk, and volatility alerts alongside prices so users can anticipate changing risk before failure.

principle: Solve the right problem before optimizing the solution.
quote: But even before this, there is one overriding principle: solve the right problem.
apply: Define the dashboard’s primary prediction-market decision (e.g., spotting mispriced contracts) and remove panels that do not support it.

principle: Design around human needs, capabilities, and usability.
quote: HCD is a procedure for addressing these requirements, but with an emphasis on two things: solving the right problem, and doing so in a way that meets human needs and capabilities.
apply: Use progressive disclosure and readable contrast in dark mode so dense odds, volumes, and charts remain understandable under real trading conditions.

principle: Iterate through observation, ideation, prototyping, and testing.
quote: iterate through the four stages of observation, generation, prototyping, and testing.
apply: Prototype dark data-dense layouts and test users on tasks like comparing contract probabilities before committing to a final hierarchy.

principle: Observe users in their real environment and workflow.
quote: observe the would-be customers in their natural environment, in their normal lives, wherever the product or service being designed will actually be used.
apply: Study prediction-market users on actual devices and multi-monitor setups to tune spacing, density, and chart interactions.

principle: Question and reframe the problem before converging.
quote: Designers often start by questioning the problem given to them: they expand the scope of the problem, diverging to examine all the fundamental issues that underlie it.
apply: For a prediction-market dashboard, first map all data and decisions users need, then converge on one clear visual hierarchy and chart set.

principle: Treat quantitative data as incomplete without human context.
quote: numerical correlations say nothing of people’s real needs, of their desires, and of the reasons for their activities.
apply: Pair market metrics with qualitative context such as event narrative, liquidity, and uncertainty rather than presenting isolated statistics as truth.

principle: Observe real use, don't rely on stated requirements.
quote: Requirements made in the abstract are invariably wrong. Requirements produced by asking people what they need are invariably wrong.
apply: Observe live trading sessions to define dashboard information hierarchy and alert thresholds, not surveys or stakeholder assumptions.

principle: Iterate with small usability tests.
quote: five people studied individually. Then, study the results, refine them, and do another iteration, testing five different people.
apply: Run 5-user tests per iteration on dark dashboard prototypes, fixing contrast, chart readability, and data density between rounds.

principle: Design around activities, not individual users.
quote: Let the activity define the product and its structure.
apply: Structure the dashboard around core prediction-market activities (scanning, comparing, forecasting, trading) for cross-user usability.

principle: Support special cases; rigid systems fail.
quote: Any system that does not allow for special cases will fail.
apply: Provide configurable filters, annotations, and chart layers for atypical market events instead of forcing one fixed view.

principle: Prototype and test before committing.
quote: The only way to really know whether an idea is reasonable is to test it. Build a quick prototype or mock-up of each potential solution.
apply: Create quick clickable prototypes of dark-mode layouts to test color semantics, type scale, and spacing before engineering build.

principle: Question inherited conventions.
quote: Question everything. I am particularly fond of “stupid” questions.
apply: Challenge standard finance-dashboard conventions (red/green, dense tables) and verify they improve prediction-market cognition and trust.

principle: Design around the user's complete activity, not isolated tasks.
quote: I emphasize the need to design for activities: designing for tasks is usually too restrictive.
apply: Organize the dashboard by prediction-market workflow—discover, analyze, trade, monitor, settle—rather than by separate widget types.

principle: Bundle required subtasks so they work together without interference.
quote: Well-designed devices will package together the various tasks that are required to support an activity, making them work seamlessly with one another
apply: Let users move from market list to probability chart to order ticket to position view without context switching or duplicate data entry.

principle: Density is acceptable when it matches the user's activity and mental model.
quote: if the design requirements are consistent with their activities, people will tolerate complexity and the requirements to learn something new
apply: Keep dense tables and order books if they mirror trader workflow, but group and label columns so complexity feels appropriate.

principle: Place critical status in the focal area to reduce eye movement.
quote: Heads-up displays mean that critical instrument panel and navigation information can be displayed in the space in front of the driver, so no eye movements are required to monitor them
apply: Pin live prices, probability shifts, open positions, and P&L in a fixed top or side rail visible without scrolling.

principle: Test early prototypes with real users to refine requirements.
quote: Early prototypes have to be tested through real interaction with the target population in order to refine the requirements.
apply: Run clickable dark-mode prototypes with prediction-market traders to validate chart contrast, hierarchy, and alert placement before build.

principle: Respect human capabilities so users accept and learn complex designs.
quote: Support the activities while being sensitive to human capabilities, and people will accept the design and learn whatever is necessary.
apply: Use accessible dark-mode contrast, legible type, and clear focus states so data-dense views feel controlled rather than hostile.

principle: Design for multiple disciplines and conflicting requirements instead of one universal view.
quote: Each of the separate disciplines has a different view of the product, each has different but specific requirements to be met.
apply: Provide role-based dashboard presets for traders, analysts, and admins so order books, probability charts, and news panels can be prioritized differently.

principle: Resolve constraints early through shared requirements before piecemeal changes weaken cohesion.
quote: If all these requirements were known at the start of the design process, a much more satisfactory resolution could have been devised.
apply: Define global dark-mode design tokens for color, type, spacing, and chart palettes before adding new market widgets.

principle: There is no average user; accommodate varied sizes, abilities, and contexts.
quote: There is no such thing as the average person.
apply: Offer comfortable/compact density modes, scalable fonts, and colorblind-safe chart palettes for data-dense market views.

principle: Accessibility should not be stigmatized or advertised as a special separate mode.
quote: Most people do not wish to advertise their infirmities. Actually, many people do not wish to admit having infirmities, even to themselves.
apply: Integrate larger type, reduced motion, and high-contrast chart settings as normal display options, not as an 'accessibility mode'.

principle: Balance what users need with what makes them act, because both matter for product success.
quote: What people need and what they buy are two different things, but both are important. It doesn’t matter how great the product is if nobody buys it.
apply: Pair deep analytical panels with clear trade actions, fees, and liquidity cues so the dashboard supports both understanding and conversion.

principle: Design must account for operational, business, and support contexts beyond the core data view.
quote: Design must take into account sales and marketing, servicing and help desks, engineering and manufacturing, costs and schedules.
apply: Surface resolution rules, fees, liquidity, settlement sources, and support links directly in the dashboard to build trader trust.

principle: Build flexibility into dense dashboards so users can adapt layouts to their needs.
quote: The best solution to the problem of designing for everyone is flexibility: flexibility in the size of the images on computer screens, in the sizes, heights, and angles of tables and chairs.
apply: Let traders resize/reorder panels, choose compact vs. comfortable density, adjust chart height, and persist these per-user settings.

principle: Use high-contrast type and larger text; it improves readability for everyone, especially in dark or dim conditions.
quote: Make the lettering larger, with high-contrast type, and everyone can read it better. In dim light, even the people with the world’s best eyesight will benefit from such lettering.
apply: In dark mode, use strong foreground/background contrast for prices, probabilities, and labels; avoid faint gray text for critical market data.

principle: Preserve necessary complexity but eliminate confusion through clear organization.
quote: complexity is essential: it is confusion that is undesirable.
apply: Don’t hide essential prediction-market depth; instead group related data, label sections clearly, and visually separate market data, order entry, and position tracking.

principle: Provide a strong conceptual model so complex data structures feel understandable.
quote: The most important principle for taming complexity is to provide a good conceptual model
apply: Model the dashboard around the user’s mental flow: market → outcome → probability/price → order/position, with consistent terms and navigation.

principle: Standardize interface patterns so learned behavior transfers across markets and views.
quote: With standardization, once you have learned to drive one car, you feel justifiably confident that you can drive any car, anyplace in the world. Standardization provides a major breakthrough in usability.
apply: Keep chart axes, color semantics, number formats, order controls, and keyboard shortcuts consistent across every market page.

principle: Allow users to adjust visual and environmental settings for comfort and accessibility.
quote: Allow people to adjust their own seats, tables, and working devices. Allow them to adjust lighting, font size, and contrast.
apply: Offer controls for font size, contrast, chart scale, column density, and dark/light themes, and remember them between sessions.

principle: Standardize interaction conventions
quote: Standardize and you simplify lives: everyone learns the system only once.
apply: Use one consistent token set for colors, chart axes, time formats, and trade actions across all prediction-market views so users learn the dashboard once.

principle: Don't lock in standards prematurely
quote: But don’t standardize too soon; you may be locked into a primitive technology, or you may have introduced rules that turn out to be grossly inefficient, even error-inducing.
apply: Keep chart/time/color conventions modular and versioned; avoid hard-coding early aspect ratios, tick labels, or interaction patterns before trading-data needs stabilize.

principle: Isolate deliberate friction
quote: Usually there is one difficult part, designed to keep unauthorized people from using the device; the rest of it should follow the normal principles of good design.
apply: For sensitive prediction-market actions, add one deliberate confirmation/2FA step, but keep market browsing, filtering, and order-book reading frictionless.

principle: Use two-step controls for high-risk actions
quote: Controls that require two simultaneous actions before the system will operate, with the controls separated so that it takes two people to work them
apply: Require hold-to-confirm or two-key/two-person approval for irreversible trades or large withdrawals; never hide routine navigation controls.

principle: Warnings can create secondary hazards
quote: The barriers solve one problem, but they themselves pose another danger, often mitigated by adding signs and flashing lights to warn of the barriers.
apply: When adding red alerts, modals, or safety overlays, include persistent legends, dismiss/escape paths, and non-obstructive placement so warnings don't obscure prices or create alert fatigue.

principle: Design for human use, not just data density
quote: the designers must always keep foremost in mind that the products are to be used by people.
apply: Optimize the dark dashboard for trader cognition and trust: high-contrast type, clear hierarchy, accessible colorblind-safe probability/price encoding, transparent data provenance, and spacing that remains legible under dense market data.

principle: Avoid featuritis in dashboards; every feature must serve a real need.
quote: Creeping featurism is the tendency to add to the number of features of a product, often extending the number beyond all reason.
apply: Require every dashboard panel/filter to map to a core prediction-market task; remove or hide features added only to match competitors.

principle: Maintain system-wide consistency, coherence, and understandability.
quote: Good design requires stepping back from competitive pressures and ensuring that the entire product be consistent, coherent, and understandable.
apply: Use one semantic color system for YES/NO, probability, liquidity, and risk across all cards/charts, with consistent typography and chart idioms.

principle: Design around human psychology and cognitive limits, not technology trends.
quote: The design of technology to fit human needs and capabilities is determined by the psychology of people.
apply: Optimize dark data-dense views for rapid probability comparison under load: pre-attentive cues, stable spatial positions, and minimal working-memory demands.

principle: Manage complexity with progressive disclosure rather than cramming more controls onscreen.
quote: Portable devices get smaller and smaller with each release, despite the addition of more and more features (making them ever more difficult to operate).
apply: Show odds, volume, expiry, and resolution risk first; tuck advanced order-book analytics into expandable drawers instead of displaying every control at once.

principle: Prioritize real user needs over competitor feature matching.
quote: The best products come from ignoring these competing voices and instead focusing on the true needs of the people who use the product.
apply: Prioritize prediction-market decisions—price discovery, liquidity, expiry, resolution risk—over adding parity widgets from other trading dashboards.

principle: Focus on strengths instead of blindly matching competitor weaknesses.
quote: The lesson is simple: don’t follow blindly; focus on strengths, not weaknesses.
apply: Make your dashboard’s strongest assets visually dominant—e.g., live odds shifts and order-book depth—rather than diluting hierarchy with parity features.

principle: Preserve familiar market conventions over novel layouts
quote: People knew QWERTY and balked at having to learn a different organization.
apply: Keep standard prediction-market table and chart conventions: time on x-axis, probability on y-axis, and stable column order, even in dark mode.

principle: Optimize dense dashboards for skimming and fast reading
quote: Reading can be done quickly: it is possible to read around three hundred words per minute and to skim, jumping ahead and back, effectively acquiring information at rates in the thousands of words per minute.
apply: Use compact aligned numerals, clear section headers, and sparklines so users can scan many markets and probabilities without reading sequentially.

principle: Support keyboard-first expert workflows
quote: The keyboard still remains the fastest way to enter words into a system
apply: Provide keyboard shortcuts and a command palette for searching markets, filtering, switching views, and placing trades quickly.

principle: Design from stable human perception, not technology fashion
quote: But because the fundamental psychology of human beings will remain unchanged, the design rules in this book will still apply.
apply: Use consistent hierarchy, spacing, and color semantics based on perception; avoid gesture-only or unfamiliar interactions for critical market actions.

principle: Use distinct visual patterns for at-a-glance recognition
quote: it only mattered that the pattern generated by the approximation to the correct path was close enough to the desired one.
apply: Encode outcomes, trends, and risk with distinct color/shape patterns so users can recognize market states quickly, while exact values remain available.

principle: Prioritize reliability and performance for trust
quote: the required robustness, versatility, and very low cost necessary for the idea to be deployed in the home consumer market.
apply: Ensure dark-mode charts, live odds, and order books render reliably and update without jank; stability builds trust in data-dense prediction markets.

principle: Respect existing mental models and legacy conventions
quote: Tradition and custom coupled with the large number of people already used to an existing scheme makes change difficult or even impossible.
apply: Keep standard prediction-market layouts (order book, price/volume panes, yes/no or up/down color semantics) and offer advanced layouts as opt-in rather than replacing familiar ones.

principle: Let human factors, not legacy technical constraints, dictate spacing and arrangement
quote: the size, spacing, and arrangement of the keys were dictated by these mechanical considerations, not by the characteristics of the human hand.
apply: Set table row height, column spacing, and numeric type size from trader scan-speed tests, not from database/table defaults.

principle: Drive layout evolution by user tasks, not marketing or internal convenience
quote: The keyboard was designed through an evolutionary process, but the main driving forces were mechanical and marketing.
apply: Prioritize probability, spread, volume, and time-to-close in the default hierarchy; move secondary metadata behind progressive disclosure.

principle: Design the details and failure states, not just the concept
quote: Thinking of the concept of a video connection was relatively easy. Thinking through the details has been very difficult,
apply: Specify loading, stale-data, empty, and error states for every chart and order-book pane, including latency and refresh cues.

principle: Reduce repetitive hand/wrist motion in dense, frequent workflows
quote: This ailment is a result of frequent and prolonged repetitive motions of the hand and wrist
apply: Add keyboard shortcuts, saved layouts, and bulk actions so traders can monitor and trade without repeated precision mouse movements.

principle: Minimize disruptive change for conservative users
quote: People are very conservative.
apply: Persist pane positions and color meanings across releases; introduce new prediction-market widgets as opt-in modules.

principle: Respect established mental models and standards unless an alternative delivers a clear, tested gain.
quote: Once a standard is in place, the vested interests of existing practices impede change, even where the change would be an improvement.
apply: Keep familiar prediction-market conventions—probability percentages, green/red outcomes, price ladders, time-series axes—rather than introducing novel color or chart encodings that force relearning.

principle: Make actions and data relationships visible; avoid hidden, memorized command systems.
quote: With a chord keyboard, you have to press several keys simultaneously. There is no way to label the keys properly and no way to know what to do just by looking.
apply: Expose critical actions (trade, filter, resolve, sort) as labeled controls in the dashboard rather than relying on multi-key shortcuts, gestures, or undocumented modal commands.

principle: Optimize dense layouts through continuous testing and incremental refinement.
quote: the design is tested, problem areas are discovered and modified, and then the product is continually retested and remodified.
apply: Continuously usability-test and A/B test dark-mode contrast, table density, chart scales, and spacing; fix readability problems incrementally instead of one-off redesigns.

principle: Design for stable human cognition even as technology changes.
quote: Technology changes rapidly, people and culture change slowly.
apply: Keep navigation, color meanings, and key data locations stable across releases so users do not have to relearn a data-dense dashboard after every update.

principle: Anchor the interface around fundamental user jobs, not visual novelty.
quote: Fundamental needs will also stay the same, even if they get satisfied in radically different ways.
apply: Make probability comparison, position/risk monitoring, and event research the primary hierarchy; treat decorative dark-mode effects and exotic visualizations as secondary.

principle: Use explicit grouping and hierarchy when dense data is broken across rows or panels.
quote: Because the letters have to be laid out in several rows, just knowing the alphabet isn’t enough. You also have to know where the rows break,
apply: In dense tables and grids, add clear section headers, row bands, and spacing rules so users can see where logical groups start and end, not just rely on alphabetical or numerical sorting.

principle: Design as a human-machine partnership, not automation replacement.
quote: Human plus machine is more powerful than either human or machine alone.
apply: Pair transparent model outputs like implied probability, liquidity, and spread with user annotations, watchlists, and manual overrides instead of hiding them.

principle: Support non-linear, modular information access.
quote: Why shouldn’t it be composed of small sections, readable in whatever order is desired?
apply: Build dashboards as rearrangeable cards or panels with saved layouts, filters, and deep links so users can jump between markets, order books, and positions in any order.

principle: Automate trivial computation to free attention for judgment.
quote: it unleashes the mind from the petty tyranny of tending to the trivial and allows it to concentrate on the important and the critical.
apply: Auto-compute implied odds, payouts, spreads, and time decay; surface only exceptions, alerts, and high-impact changes in the primary view.

principle: Prioritize use over desire in visual design.
quote: We are surrounded with objects of desire, not objects of use.
apply: For data-dense dark dashboards, favor high-contrast typography, muted chrome, and semantic color only for up/down/risk states over decorative gradients or animations.

principle: Signal authoritative, verified data.
quote: where the facts have been checked and the message authoritative, where the material will flow, experts are needed.
apply: Attach source, timestamp, resolution criteria, and update latency to each market or chart; visually distinguish verified data from user-generated or stale data.

principle: Avoid manipulative design and opaque assumptions.
quote: The conscious manipulation of society has severe drawbacks, not the least of which is the fact that not everyone agrees on the appropriate goals.
apply: Make fees, slippage, resolution sources, and risk metrics explicit; avoid dark patterns that nudge trades or obscure downside probabilities.

principle: Prioritize discoverability and feedback through signifiers, mapping, and conceptual models
quote: the principles of discoverability, of feedback, and of the power of affordances and signifiers, mapping, and conceptual models will always hold.
apply: Use consistent hover/focus/active states, visible order-book actions, and color-coded Yes/No outcome signifiers with legends that explain mapping.

principle: Avoid superfluous, overloaded, unnecessary interface elements
quote: The design of everyday things is in great danger of becoming the design of superfluous, overloaded, unnecessary things.
apply: Strip decorative panels and duplicate metrics; use progressive disclosure so core probability, price, volume, and liquidity remain scannable.

principle: Design the dashboard as a total experience, not just a data display
quote: In other words, the design must be thought of as a total experience.
apply: Unify dark-theme colors, typography, spacing, and chart styles so scanning odds, time series, and market depth feels coherent and trustworthy.

principle: Small details materially affect usability and trust in dense interfaces
quote: Realize that even details matter, that the designer may have had to fight to include something helpful.
apply: Align numeric columns, use tabular figures, ensure sufficient contrast, and label axes precisely so dense market data stays readable.

principle: User difficulty indicates bad design, not user error
quote: If you have difficulties, remember, it’s not your fault: it’s bad design.
apply: Add inline definitions, empty-state guidance, and trade-ticket error prevention so users do not misread probabilities or place wrong orders.

principle: Support the full product lifecycle with assistance and clarity
quote: products have a complex life cycle. Many people will need assistance in using a device
apply: Provide contextual tooltips, documentation, and data-provenance notes for market-resolution rules and chart metrics.
